title: The medieval church
premise: The surviving record of the church from the council of Chalcedon in 451 to about 1350 is mostly written from the top, by popes, councils, kings and bishops, so a reader has to ask of each sentence whether it says what someone wanted or what people did. Where a war or a trial was written down by more than one side, the question can be asked twice.
question: Who wrote this down, and how far did it reach?
outcomes: Tell what a council, pope or king decreed from what the record shows happened next.
Keep a baptised ruler apart from a believing people, and say who wrote the story and how long after.
Follow how popes and kings each claimed the upper hand, and name the event that tested the claim.
Tell the long parting of East and West from the year it is remembered by, and say what Lyon and Florence agreed and why neither held.
Read a crusade or a heresy trial through each side's witness, and say what each could know.
Read a disputed question in its five moves, and say what a student had to do to reach it.
Walk a parish church from gate to altar, naming the rule at each step and how little shows whether it was kept.

boundaries.in: From the council of Chalcedon in 451 to about 1350 in the Latin West: the conversion of northern Europe, popes and kings, the long parting from the Greek East (followed on to the council of Florence in 1439), the crusades and the inquisition, the universities and their method, and ordinary parish life.
out: The councils up to Chalcedon, the rise of monasticism and the creeds: The early church. Monks appear here only as missionaries and scholars.
1350 to 1517, with the Great Schism of the popes, Wycliffe, the Lollards and Hus: The Reformation and the awakenings. Only the thread between East and West runs on here, to Florence.
How medieval readers read the Bible, including the four senses: How the church has read the Bible.
The Baptist line and what the traditions share today: Baptist history.
Jews and Christians across the centuries has no study here. The killings of 1096 appear because the crusade record needs them.
What each thinker taught and what councils defined. Aquinas appears for the form of his argument, the Fourth Lateran Council for what it asked of priests, parishes and judges of heresy.
What worship and the sacraments meant to those who took part. The parish section reports rules and records only.

fields.name: Mission
fields.note: Who was baptised, and what changed

fields.name: Parish
fields.note: What priests and people were told

pairs.head: Keep the temple. Break the idol.

declared.who: Pope Gregory I, to Abbot Mellitus, going to Kent
declared.quote: the temples of the idols in that nation ought not to be destroyed; but let the idols that are in them be destroyed

followed.who: King Rædwald of the East Angles, as Bede tells it
followed.quote: in the same temple he had an altar to sacrifice to Christ, and another small one to offer victims to devils

pairs.evidence: Gregory's letter survives in Bede (book 1, chapter 30) and argues that people rise “by degrees or steps, and not by leaps”. Bede (book 2, chapter 15) says Rædwald was baptised in Kent and then kept two altars in one temple, which a later king had seen as a boy.
pairs.inference: This study sets the two side by side because they show the same ground from two ends. A slow change can look patient from Rome and like two altars from East Anglia.
pairs.limit: Rædwald's temple is not a result of Gregory's letter: nothing connects them, so the thread here is dashed. Bede gives no year for it, so the range runs from about the time of his baptism to his death. Bede wrote over a century later and disapproved.

pairs.head: Baptism or death. Then revolt.

declared.quote: shall have scorned to come to baptism and shall have wished to remain a pagan, let him be punished by death

followed.who: The same king, and the Saxons
followed.what: Wars and risings run on to 804. In 797 Charlemagne himself eases the special laws.

pairs.evidence: The capitulary's eighth chapter makes refusing baptism a capital crime; its fourteenth lets a secret offender who confesses to a priest escape death. Alcuin, at the king's court, wrote about 796 that a person can be drawn into the faith, not forced.
pairs.inference: The law shows what the conqueror wanted. The easing and the long wars suggest it did not get it by that road. This study does not claim Alcuin's letter caused the change.
pairs.limit: A law does not record how often it was used. The law's date is itself a range here, and the English comes from a 1900 translation. The record of the Saxons' own thinking is close to nil: nearly everything comes from the Frankish side.

pairs.head: One law. Sacrifice in secret.

declared.who: The Icelandic assembly, on the law-speaker's ruling
declared.quote: all people had to be Christian and accept baptism

followed.who: The same ruling, and its exceptions
followed.quote: People had to make sacrifices in secret, if they wanted to avoid three-year outlawry

pairs.evidence: Ari Thorgilsson, writing over a century later, says the ruling kept exposing infants and eating horse-meat as they were, and allowed sacrifice in private unless there were witnesses. He adds that “a few years later, that heathen practice was also taken away”.
pairs.inference: Here baptism arrived as a settlement between factions, to keep one law in one land. The exceptions name what the settlement left alone.
pairs.limit: Ari is the earliest account and writes from a Christian bishop's world. He gives no year for the later change, so the range drawn here is this study's and only says “a few years”. The English is a volunteer translation on Wikisource.

pairs.head: May depose emperors. Dies in exile.

declared.who: The Dictates of the Pope, in Gregory VII's register
declared.quote: That it may be permitted to him to depose emperors.

followed.what: Henry stands a penitent at Canossa in 1077, and enters Rome in 1084. Gregory leaves with the Normans and dies at Salerno in 1085.

pairs.evidence: The list also says the pope “may be judged by no one”. Gregory deposed Henry in 1076. Henry was absolved at Canossa in January 1077, entered Rome in March 1084 and was crowned by an opposing pope; Gregory died at Salerno in May 1085.
pairs.inference: Each side had a real weapon. Gregory could strip a king of his princes' loyalty for a time, and Henry could take Rome. The claim held on parchment, and was only partly true on the road to Salerno.
pairs.limit: Some scholars date the list's compiling later than 1075, and it may not be Gregory's own writing. Whether Canossa was a king's humiliation or his clever escape is argued: it restored him to the church and undercut the princes against him. This study knows that argument through reference articles and names no side.

pairs.head: A king's rules. A dead archbishop.

declared.who: Henry II of England, the Constitutions of Clarendon
declared.what: Sixteen articles curb church courts and appeals to Rome.

followed.who: Thomas Becket, and Henry at Avranches
followed.what: Becket opposes them and is killed in his cathedral in 1170. At Avranches in 1172 Henry gives up the customs the church objected to.

pairs.evidence: Popes were not the only ones to write rules. After Becket's murder, Henry was cleared of guilt at Avranches in 1172, agreed to allow appeals to Rome and gave up the customs the church objected to.
pairs.inference: A paper can fail from the king's side as well. This pair is here so that the pattern is not read as being only about popes.
pairs.limit: This study read about these through reference articles, not the chroniclers. How far Henry's concessions changed daily practice in English courts is not something those articles settle.

pairs.head: Every creature subject. Then Anagni.

declared.who: Pope Boniface VIII, the bull Unam Sanctam
declared.quote: it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff

followed.who: Philip IV's men, and the popes after
followed.what: In 1303 the French king's adviser and Sciarra Colonna seize the pope at Anagni. In 1309 the papal court moves to Avignon.

pairs.evidence: Nogaret, the French king's adviser, and Sciarra Colonna seized the pope at Anagni in 1303. Townspeople freed him after about three days, and he died in Rome that October. From 1309 seven popes in turn resided at Avignon, until 1376.
pairs.inference: The highest claim in this period's record and one of its plainest defeats fall a year apart. So how high a claim is written does not show how far it reached.
pairs.limit: Avignon was not French land at the time, and how far those popes were the crown's men is argued, so “defeat” describes Anagni better than Avignon. The slap of Anagni is a legend.

pairs.head: Not to be read. Then required.

declared.who: Cardinal Robert de Courçon, statutes for the masters at Paris
declared.quote: The books of Aristotle on Metaphysics or Natural Philosophy, or the abridgements of these works, are not to be read

followed.who: Pope Gregory IX, and the Paris masters of arts
followed.what: In 1231 the ban is kept only until the books are cleared of error. In 1255 the masters of arts set the Physics and the Metaphysics on their list.

pairs.evidence: In 1231 Gregory IX kept the ban only until the books were cleared of error. In 1255 the masters of arts set the Physics and the Metaphysics on their list of texts.
pairs.inference: The rule went one way and the school the other, within forty years.
pairs.limit: The ban bound lecturing at Paris only. The bishop of Paris condemned 219 theses in 1277, so the argument did not end in 1255.

pairs.head: A master in every cathedral. Not observed.

declared.who: The Third Lateran Council, as the Fourth reports it
declared.quote: in every cathedral church a suitable benefice be assigned to a master

followed.who: The Fourth Lateran Council, on the same rule
followed.quote: But, since in many churches this is not observed

pairs.evidence: Canon 11 of 1215 quotes the older rule, says many churches do not keep it, confirms it and widens it.
pairs.inference: A council is the witness that its own earlier rule had not reached.
pairs.limit: “Many churches” is the council's phrase, with no count, and it does not say which.

pairs.head: Prepare your priests. “Pater, for He governeth all things.”

declared.quote: If in the future they presume to ordain ignorant and unformed men

followed.who: The dean of Salisbury's visit to Sonning, and the curate Simon
followed.quote: He knew not the case of Te, nor by what word it was governed

pairs.evidence: Seven years after the canon, a dean examined a curate ordained about four years earlier. Simon could not understand the Gospel he read or parse the opening words of the prayer of the Mass, and thought it indecent to be examined. The clerk's note ends: “He is amply illiterate.”
pairs.inference: A rule made in Rome in 1215 had not settled who stood at the altar in a Berkshire village in 1222.
pairs.limit: One man is not a clergy. Such records exist to find faults, and they are also the evidence that someone was checking.

pairs.head: Live chastely. “Ill-famed of incontinence.”

declared.quote: let all strive to live chastely and virtuously, particularly those in sacred orders

followed.who: Archbishop Odo Rigaud, visiting his own cathedral at Rouen
followed.quote: many other of the statutes written on the board in the vestry are not kept

pairs.evidence: Odo's register names canons of Rouen as ill-famed of incontinence, tavern-going, dicing and trading, and sets a date for correction.
pairs.inference: The problem reached the head of a province a generation on, and so did a reformer who wrote it down.
pairs.limit: “Ill-famed” means reported, not proved. One cathedral on one day, under Parish because the same rules reached every parish's clergy.

pairs.head: Confess each year. Teach them what to confess.

declared.quote: All the faithful of both sexes shall after they have reached the age of discretion faithfully confess all their sins at least once a year

followed.who: Archbishop John Pecham's council at Lambeth
followed.what: English priests are told to explain the faith to their people, in their own tongue, four times a year.

pairs.evidence: Sixty-six years on, Pecham's council, known by its opening words Ignorantia sacerdotum (the ignorance of priests), told English priests to explain the creed, the commandments, the works of mercy, the deadly sins, the virtues and the sacraments in the people's tongue four times a year.
pairs.inference: A yearly duty needs a people who know what it asks. The decree of 1281 reads as the long second half of the rule of 1215.
pairs.limit: A decree that names ignorance is a reformer's opening, not a survey. This study read reports of it, not its Latin.

stations.name: The Franks
stations.head: “Burn what you worshipped.”
stations.text: King Clovis asks for baptism, and the bishop tells him: “worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.” Clovis took the Catholic faith where most Germanic rulers held the Arian one.
stations.limit: Gregory writes about ninety years on and casts Clovis as “another Constantine”. Modern dates range over several years.

stations.name: Kent
stations.head: “Voluntary, not by compulsion.”
stations.text: Gregory sends Augustine and his monks to King Æthelberht. Bede says the king favoured those who believed but “compelled none”, having learned “that the service of Christ ought to be voluntary, not by compulsion”.
stations.limit: Bede writes over 130 years later, wanting a model. How many in Kent were baptised, and how soon, no one can say.

stations.name: Northumbria
stations.head: A sparrow through the hall.
stations.text: King Edwin puts the matter to his council. One chief man likens this life to “the swift flight of a sparrow through the room wherein you sit at supper in winter”, and says that if the new teaching holds something more certain, it should be followed. Edwin is baptised at York.
stations.limit: Bede composes the speech a century on. It shows what he thought a good reason for conversion was.

stations.name: Hesse
stations.head: He cut down the oak.
stations.text: Boniface, an English monk, fells a tree sacred to the people of Hesse as a crowd looks on, and builds a chapel from its timber. He was killed in Frisia in 754, still at the mission in old age.
stations.limit: A saint's life, within living memory. The date is reconstructed, and the Life itself says some kept sacrificing.

stations.name: Saxony
stations.head: Drawn, and not forced.
stations.text: Thirty-two years of campaigns and risings ended with Saxony inside the Frankish realm. Alcuin wrote about 796: “Attrahi poterit homo in fidem, non cogi”: a person can be drawn into the faith, not forced. Baptism could be forced, he says, and it would do nothing for faith.
stations.limit: Alcuin in the same breath excepts infants, who may be saved by others' confession, so he is not arguing for believer's baptism. A modern paper argues he did not object to the armies themselves: this study knows it only through a listing.

stations.name: Denmark
stations.head: “And made the Danes Christian.”
stations.text: King Harald raises a stone for his parents and adds his own record: he “won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian”. Ansgar had preached in Denmark over a century before, with little that lasted.
stations.limit: A boast in the king's own voice, cut in granite while he lived. The Danes left no reply.

stations.name: Poland
stations.head: A duke and his court.
stations.text: Duke Mieszko I is baptised with much of his court, and Poland counted its millennium from it in 1966. His wife, Dobrawa of Bohemia, is often credited with a large part. Spreading it through the land took far longer.
stations.limit: The place is disputed, Poznań and Gniezno the likeliest, so the mark is hollow: it stands for the country, not a known spot. The first chronicler's date is approximate.

stations.name: Iceland
stations.head: One law, to keep the peace.
stations.text: The two parties at the assembly were close to fighting. The law-speaker Thorgeir, himself a pagan priest, took a day and a night apart, then ruled that all should be baptised, because to tear the law would tear the peace.
stations.limit: Ari wrote about 125 years later. The story of Thorgeir throwing his idols into a waterfall is not in him, and appears to be a nineteenth-century addition.

stations.name: Norway
stations.head: Two kings named Olaf.
stations.text: Olaf Tryggvason pressed the faith by every means from 995. After he fell in 1000 the old ways returned in part. Olaf Haraldsson pressed it again, and died in battle at Stiklestad in 1030.
stations.limit: The fullest accounts are sagas written about two centuries on, with a saint to honour. The figure given for when they were written is a round one.

stations.name: Sweden
stations.head: Over two hundred years on, a temple is still described.
stations.text: Ansgar reached Birka in the 830s. About 1075 Adam of Bremen still describes a great temple at Uppsala, with Thor, Odin and Freyr enthroned. Sweden's archdiocese came only in 1164.
stations.limit: Adam wrote from Bremen, on reports and with a cause, and the temple as he describes it is now questioned.

stations.name: Prussia
stations.head: A crusade for a mission.
stations.text: A bishop's preaching failed, and the Teutonic Knights were invited in. Half a century of war followed. The people who were conquered did not write their own account.
stations.limit: Peter of Dusburg, the Order's chronicler, wrote about 1326 for the Order. The Prussian language later died out and there is no account from the other side.

missionStand.head: Where this site stands
missionStand.text: This site holds with the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 that “God alone is Lord of the conscience”, and that baptism is the immersion of a believer. So it reads a ruler's baptism and a forced one as history, and does not count either as a people's coming to faith. It says so of Charlemagne and of Harald, and it gives thanks for those who came preaching. Who among these people truly believed is not something the record can show, in either direction.

rounds.why: A claim in a letter, with nothing yet tested.
rounds.limit: Gelasius wrote as one party. The letter does not say how the emperor took it.
rounds.head: Two powers named.
rounds.text: “There are two powers, august Emperor, by which this world is chiefly ruled”: the priests' authority and the royal power. He adds that the priests' is the more weighty. This is a claim and not yet a contest.

rounds.why: Each side gained what it could not get alone.
rounds.limit: Read through a reference article and not the chroniclers.
rounds.head: Each makes the other.
rounds.text: Pippin takes the Frankish crown in 751 with the popes' backing, and in 756 hands the pope lands in central Italy: territory and a protector for one, a blessing on a new dynasty for the other.

rounds.why: Both readings of that crown stayed open.
rounds.limit: Einhard admired the king and wrote after his death. The king's dislike is his report, and cannot be tested.
rounds.head: Who crowned whom?
rounds.text: On Christmas Day at Rome the pope crowns Charlemagne emperor. Einhard says the king so disliked the titles “that he would not have set foot in the Church” had he foreseen the pope's design. A crown from a pope could later be read either way.

rounds.why: A king's army settled who was pope.
rounds.limit: Read through a reference article and not the synod's own record.
rounds.head: An emperor sorts out the popes.
rounds.text: Three men claim the papacy. Henry III crosses the Alps with an army, calls a synod at Sutri and has a German bishop made pope, who crowns him. The reformers who later opposed kings first rose with a king's help.

rounds.why: A king came as a penitent, to a pope's terms.
rounds.limit: Some read it as Henry's clever escape, since being absolved undercut the princes against him. See the record for that pair.
rounds.head: A king at the gate.
rounds.text: Gregory excommunicates and deposes Henry, and German princes turn on him. In January 1077 Henry waits three days at Canossa as a penitent and is absolved. In the picture he kneels to ask Matilda of Tuscany and Abbot Hugh to speak for him.

rounds.why: The king held the city, and the pope left with his rescuers.
rounds.limit: Gregory never gave up the claim, and popes after him kept it.
rounds.head: A king at the walls.
rounds.text: Seven years on, Henry enters Rome, an opposing pope crowns him, and Gregory dies at Salerno. Canossa is the scene people remember. It was not the end of the story.

rounds.why: Each side kept something it could name as the point.
rounds.limit: It settled terms for the Empire. England had made its own arrangement earlier.
rounds.head: Ring and staff for one, sceptre for the other.
rounds.text: The emperor surrenders “all investiture through ring and staff”, the signs of a bishop's spiritual office. The pope grants that elections in Germany take place in the emperor's presence, and that the bishop takes his lands by the sceptre. Both can claim the day.

rounds.why: The king gave up on paper what he had fought for.
rounds.limit: How far Avranches changed daily practice in English courts is not settled by what this study read.
rounds.head: A murder changes the terms.
rounds.text: Henry's rules of 1164 are opposed by his archbishop, who is killed in 1170. At Avranches in 1172 the king accepts appeals to Rome. A dead archbishop did what a living one could not.

rounds.why: A king formally held his kingdom from the pope.
rounds.limit: It was John's own bargain, and it served him.
rounds.head: A kingdom held from Rome.
rounds.text: After years under interdict, and fearing a French invasion, John surrenders England to the papacy and takes it back for 1,000 marks a year, gaining a powerful ally.

rounds.why: The king's men laid hands on the pope, and he died that year.
rounds.limit: Townspeople freed him within days, and this study does not say the bull alone caused the attack.
rounds.head: The highest claim, and a palace stormed.
rounds.text: Unam Sanctam reads “two swords” from the disciples' words in Luke and puts both in the church's power. A year later the king's men hold the pope captive at Anagni.

rounds.why: French popes, close to the French crown.
rounds.limit: The town was not French, and how far those popes were the crown's men is argued.
rounds.head: The court moves north.
rounds.text: The papal court settles at Avignon under seven French popes. The town lay inside the Empire and was bought by the pope in 1348, so this was not simply captivity. The tilt here is this study's least certain call.

roundsNote: Each tilt is this study's judgement of who came out ahead in that one event, not a measurement. The same event was read in opposite ways at the time and since. Nothing here adds up to a score.

powersStand.head: Where this site stands
powersStand.text: Scripture tells believers to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, and the disciples' “two swords” answer a moment on the road to the garden and name no office. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 holds that church and state are to be separate, and calls “A free church in a free state” the Christian ideal, so this site stands with neither pope nor king in these contests. Unam Sanctam makes subjection to the pope necessary for salvation. Baptists do not hold that: Scripture names Christ as the head of the church. Catholic teaching on the papacy is reported here as its own.

split.lead: Rome and Constantinople did not part in a day. The upper line is the Latin church, the lower the Greek: a rung means communion, a gap means none, and a knot is a union agreed and undone. Choose a step.
split.note: Whether the churches counted as in communion between 1054 and 1204 is a matter of reading, so the rungs fade there instead of stopping.

steps.head: Second after Rome. Rome says no.
steps.text: Canon 28 of Chalcedon ranked Constantinople next after Rome, because the city was “honored with the Sovereignty and the Senate”. Pope Leo I confirmed the council's teaching and {{check:c1}}declared the canon null and void in 453{{/check}}.
steps.inference: From 451 a church could be ranked by the apostle who founded it or by its city's place in the empire. Much of what follows is that quarrel.
steps.limit: Quoted from a reference article's translation. The East kept the canon.

steps.head: Thirty-five years apart.
steps.text: Rome excommunicated Patriarch Acacius in 484 for accepting Emperor Zeno's Henotikon, a statement meant to reconcile those who rejected Chalcedon. The churches stayed apart until Easter 519.
steps.inference: The first long break came over Chalcedon's own teaching, centuries before 1054, and it was mended.
steps.limit: Read through a reference article, not the letters.

steps.head: A patriarch, a pope and Bulgaria.
steps.text: Pope Nicholas I refused to recognise Photius as patriarch. Photius attacked the Latin missionaries in Bulgaria, baptised from Constantinople {{check:c2}}in about 864 or 865{{/check}}, for teaching the creed with “and the Son”, and a synod in 867 declared the pope deposed. A council in 879 and 880 reconciled the sees.
steps.inference: Three later grievances are here: a pope's authority over a patriarch, the clause on the Spirit, and whose missionaries a new people would follow.
steps.limit: Rome itself did not yet say the clause in 867. Read through reference articles.

steps.head: Two sentences in one week.
steps.text: On 16 July 1054 papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert laid a sentence of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch's synod answered in kind. Pope Leo IX, who had sent them, was already dead.
steps.inference: The sentences fell on persons, not churches: 1054 is the year remembered, not the day of parting. {{check:c3}}In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I removed them “from memory and from the midst of the Church”, and said this did not end the differences.{{/check}}
steps.limit: The two sentences were not read; the dates come from reports. Historians propose other dates for the real break, among them 1204.

steps.head: Crusaders take Constantinople.
steps.text: The Fourth Crusade, in debt to Venice, took Zara, a Christian city, in 1202 and sacked Constantinople in April 1204. Niketas Choniates, who lived through it, calls the crusaders {{check:c4}}“wrathful barbarians”{{/check}}. Latins held the city until 1261.
steps.inference: Many historians weigh 1204 above 1054: a quarrel of bishops became a people's memory of plunder. {{check:c5}}Innocent III, who had forbidden attacks on Christians, rebuked the crusaders, and still accepted the Latin church set up in the city.{{/check}}
steps.limit: Choniates is read in a short excerpt; Innocent's letters were not read.

steps.head: A union signed for an emperor.
steps.text: At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, envoys of Emperor Michael VIII accepted union, the clause and the pope's primacy; Michael needed the pope to hold back a Western attack. {{check:c6}}Most Greek clergy and people rejected it, and Andronikos II renounced it after 1282.{{/check}}
steps.inference: A union agreed by a ruler's envoys, for a ruler's reasons, did not reach the churches it spoke for.
steps.limit: From reports only; no text of the council was read.

steps.head: “The wall … has been removed.”
steps.text: On 6 July 1439 the decree of union said that “the wall that divided the western and the eastern church has been removed”, and that the clause was “licitly and reasonably added to the creed”. {{check:c7}}Every Greek bishop present signed except Mark of Ephesus, and Constantinople refused the union{{/check}}; the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
steps.inference: Churches still negotiating union in 1439 had not finished parting in 1054. Florence lies past this study's end and is followed because the thread ends there.
steps.limit: The decree was read through a report. Mark's refusal is the usual account, not checked here.

stand.head: Where this site stands
stand.text: Jesus speaks of the Spirit “who proceeds from the Father”, whom He will send. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 does not speak to the clause “and the Son”; the Baptist confession of 1689 says it with the West, and the Eastern churches keep the creed of 381 without it. This site does not settle that argument. Baptists claim neither Rome's primacy nor Constantinople's, for Christ is head of the church, and this site counts the sack of 1204 as a wrong done by Christians to Christians.

crusade.lead: The crusades and the heresy trials are among the few medieval events written down by more than one side. Choose an event. A filled mark means a witness from that side survives and is used here.
crusade.sidesNote: A witness is a written account from that side. Many wrote decades later, and each says when.

events.head: A sermon with no text.
events.text: At Clermont Pope Urban II called knights to go east, help the Christians there and free Jerusalem, the journey to count as penance for their sins. {{check:c8}}No text survives: Fulcher of Chartres, probably present, and three others each wrote a version between about 1101 and 1110.{{/check}}
events.inference: The call is known through what its hearers made of it.
events.limit: This study read none of the versions whole.

witnesses.who: Fulcher of Chartres and three others

events.head: “The bishop himself fled.”
events.text: Before the main armies left, bands led by Emicho, a German noble, attacked the Jews of Speyer, Worms and Mainz. Many were killed, and many killed their own families rather than be forcibly baptised. At Mainz, Solomon bar Samson writes, “the bishop himself fled from his church”.
events.inference: No pope called for this, and some bishops resisted it. It was still done by men wearing the cross, and the fuller record is the Jewish one.
events.limit: Solomon wrote about 1140, read here in a 1938 selection. {{check:c9}}The bishop of Speyer's protection and Albert of Aachen's condemnation are reported, not read.{{/check}}

witnesses.says: Names the dead, and those who chose death over baptism.

events.head: “Up to their ankles.”
events.text: The Gesta Francorum, by a man of the army, says “our men waded in blood up to their ankles”, and Fulcher of Chartres writes of “our feet colored to our ankles with the blood of the slain”. {{check:c10}}Ibn al-Athir, a century later, gives seventy thousand killed at the al-Aqsa mosque, far too high a figure; letters from Jews in Egypt tell of captives ransomed.{{/check}}
events.inference: Both sides record a massacre. The crusaders' writers tell it as a victory, not a crime.
events.limit: The Latin is from English selections of 1912 and 1921; the Arabic and Hebrew were not read.

witnesses.who: The Gesta Francorum; Fulcher of Chartres
witnesses.says: Tell it as the crown of the march.
A number too large to trust.

events.head: Mercy at the gate. Not on the field.
events.text: {{check:c11}}After Hattin, Saladin had the captured knights of the Temple and the Hospital put to death, as his secretary Imad ad-Din recorded. In October he took Jerusalem by agreement and let its Christians buy their freedom; many who could not pay were enslaved.{{/check}}
events.inference: The Muslim record praises the sultan's mercy and records the killing of prisoners. Neither side's history is only the other's crimes.
events.limit: From reference articles; Imad ad-Din was not read.

witnesses.says: Both the executions and the terms.

events.head: The legate's own count.
events.text: Innocent III called a crusade against the Cathars of southern France, judged heretics, after his legate was murdered in 1208. At Béziers the legate Arnaud Amalric reported to the pope that his men “put to the sword almost 20,000 people”. “Kill them all; the Lord knows His own” was written by Caesarius of Heisterbach about 1220, by no one present.
events.inference: The legate's boast is the harsher witness. The famous sentence is likely not his, and turns Paul's words, “The Lord knows those who are His”, to the opposite use.
events.limit: Historians think the figure far too high. Known here through a reference article. No Cathar account of Béziers survives.

witnesses.says: A legate's boast; a monk's later story.

events.head: Bishops first. Then friars with a commission.
events.text: In 1184 Pope Lucius III told bishops to seek out heretics. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council told rulers to expel those the church condemned. From about 1231 Gregory IX sent judges, mostly Dominican friars, to try heresy on his authority.
events.inference: The church judged and the ruler punished, so clergy could say they shed no blood while the punishment followed their verdict.
events.limit: {{check:c12}}That there was no single “Inquisition” then, only commissioned inquisitors, is the view of historians such as Edward Peters; older writers such as Henry Charles Lea drew a darker, more unified picture.{{/check}}

witnesses.says: The decrees that set up the courts.

events.head: Inquisitors killed. Then a pyre.
events.text: {{check:c13}}In May 1242 men from the Cathar stronghold of Montségur killed the inquisitor William Arnaud and his companions at Avignonet. When Montségur surrendered in March 1244, about two hundred Cathars who would not renounce their faith were burned.{{/check}}
events.inference: Violence ran both ways, not evenly: the inquisitors had courts and kings, the Cathars a fortress. This page reports both killings.
events.limit: From reference articles. The Cathars' side survives mostly as the inquisitors recorded it.

witnesses.says: Their words, as the court's notaries wrote them.

events.head: Torture allowed, with a limit.
events.text: Innocent IV's bull Ad extirpanda let Italian city authorities torture suspected heretics to make them confess and name others, short of danger to life or limb.
events.inference: A limit written into a licence shows what its writer knew it could lead to, not that the limit was kept.

events.head: 636 convicted. No more than 45 executed.
events.text: Bernard Gui, inquisitor at Toulouse from 1307 to 1323, wrote a handbook for inquisitors. {{check:c14}}His tribunals convicted 636 people: 307 were imprisoned, many were made to wear crosses, and no more than 45 were executed.{{/check}} At Pamiers from 1318 to 1325 Bishop Jacques Fournier had villagers' answers taken down in detail.
events.inference: The numbers are smaller than the popular picture, and they are still people burned for what they believed. This site says both. The villagers' voices survive because their judge's notaries wrote them down.
events.limit: {{check:c15}}Fournier's register is known here through reference articles and Le Roy Ladurie's Montaillou (1975), not read.{{/check}}

witnesses.says: Their answers, in the bishop's register.

debate.head: How historians read the crusades
debate.text: Historians disagree. {{check:c16}}Jonathan Riley-Smith reads the first crusaders as moved chiefly by penitent devotion, at ruinous cost; older writers stress land, plunder and papal power; Christopher Tyerman stresses how mixed and changing the movement was.{{/check}} This page reports what each witness wrote and does not choose.

stand.head: Where this site stands
stand.text: Jesus told Peter to put his sword away, and told Pilate that His kingdom “is not of this world”. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 holds that God alone is Lord of the conscience, that the church should not use the civil power to do its work, and that the state may not punish religious opinions. So this site counts the killings of 1096, the burnings for heresy and torture as wrongs done in Christ's name, as plainly as it reports prisoners killed by the crusaders' enemies. It does not judge each crusader's faith: many went at great cost, believing they served God.

article.cite: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, First Part, question 2, article 3, about 1265 to 1274
article.note: Aquinas's words in the English Dominican translation, shortened where three dots show. Shown for how the argument is built: this site's ground for belief in God is Scripture, not his five ways.

parts.name: Whether God exists?
parts.does: It asks as an open question what the writer believes with his whole life. The form requires it.

parts.name: There is evil
parts.text: It seems that God does not exist; because if one of two contraries be infinite, the other would be altogether destroyed … there is evil in the world. Therefore God does not exist.
parts.does: The other side goes first, in its strongest short form.

parts.name: Nature is enough
parts.text: … it seems that everything we see in the world can be accounted for by other principles, supposing God did not exist.
parts.does: A second, different objection. It still reads as current.

parts.name: “I am Who am”
parts.text: It is said in the person of God: “I am Who am.” (Exodus 3:14)
parts.does: One authority against the objections, here Scripture. It shows there is a question, and does not yet argue.

parts.name: Five ways
parts.text: The existence of God can be proved in five ways.
parts.does: The master's own decision: from motion, causes, what need not exist, degrees of good, and the order of things.

parts.name: Good out of evil
parts.text: As Augustine says … “He would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil.”
parts.does: He answers the first objection, by name.

parts.name: Nature has a cause
parts.text: Since nature works for a determinate end under the direction of a higher agent, whatever is done by nature must needs be traced back to God, as to its first cause.
parts.does: He answers the second. No objection is left standing.

abelard.text: The form did not begin with Aquinas. About 1120 Peter Abelard's Sic et Non (Yes and No) set authorities side by side where they seemed to disagree, for the student to work through.
abelard.quote: through doubting we come to questioning and through questions we perceive the truth

ladder.note: From the statutes of 1215. The ages are the statute's minimums. What it does not name, such as the age a boy began, this study works back, hatched on the drawing.

steps.name: Listen in arts
steps.text: “He is to listen in arts at least six years”: about fourteen, at the earliest.

steps.name: Lecture in arts
steps.text: “No one is to lecture at Paris in arts before he is twenty years old”, for at least two years.

steps.name: Study theology
steps.text: Eight years of theology, five of them listening: the statute fixes the length and the age at the end.

steps.name: Lecture in theology
steps.text: “no one shall lecture at Paris before he is thirty-five years old”, with no upper limit.

schools.name: Bologna
schools.note: The 1088 date was fixed in the 1800s. The student guilds appear in the late 1100s.

schools.name: Paris
schools.note: Grew out of the cathedral school.

schools.name: Oxford
schools.note: Grew when Henry II barred English students from Paris. Alfred's founding is a legend.

schools.name: Cambridge
schools.note: Scholars leaving Oxford after a dispute.

schoolStand.head: Where this site stands
schoolStand.text: The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 treats sound learning as part of the Christian inheritance, under “the pre-eminence of Jesus Christ” and the authority of Scripture. So this site can admire a method that hears the other side first, without taking on the Roman Catholic teaching Aquinas's work carries.

parish.note: An illustrative plan, not one church: a village church in the Latin West after about 1200. Many were smaller, and nearly all changed.

stations.name: The churchyard
stations.rule: If you did not confess yearly and receive at Easter, you were “cut off from the Church … during life and deprived of Christian burial in death”. Canon 21, 1215.
stations.record: The church could withhold this ground, and the council used it.
stations.limit: No count of refused graves was found.

stations.name: The church door
stations.rule: Marriages “must be announced publicly in the churches by the priests”, and secret marriages are forbidden. Canon 51, 1215.
stations.record: The canon extends “the particular custom that prevails in some” places, so the banns began as a local habit.
stations.limit: The church-court records that would show secret marriages were located, not read.

stations.name: The font
stations.rule: Canon 1 says baptism is for “children and adults” alike, and anyone may give it in the right form. Canon 20 keeps the chrism and the Eucharist under lock and key. Both 1215.
stations.record: This study takes infant baptism to be the ordinary practice of the time, which the canon allows and does not state. So a whole parish could be baptised without being asked.
stations.limit: How soon after birth, parish by parish, this study did not read.
stations.stand: Baptists hold that baptism is the immersion of a believer who has personally trusted Christ, and find no infant baptism in the New Testament: Scripture pictures it as burial and rising with Christ, and the command is to baptize disciples. That is this site's view. The practice here is reported as the medieval church's.

stations.name: The nave wall
stations.rule: “What writing presents to readers, this a picture presents to the unlearned who behold.” Gregory I, about 600, to a bishop of Marseilles who had broken images.
stations.record: Gregory praises him for forbidding the images to be adored and blames him for breaking them: a picture was to teach, not to be worshipped.
stations.limit: What a villager took from a painted wall, nobody wrote down, and most surviving wall paintings are later.

stations.name: The chancel arch
stations.rule: Bishops must “diligently prepare and instruct” those they ordain (canon 27) and provide preachers (canon 10), both 1215. In 1281 Pecham's priests were to teach in the people's tongue four times a year.
stations.record: In 1222 Simon at Sonning could read the Mass and not construe it. Any teaching in the people's language came from the priest in front of this arch.
stations.limit: Parish sermons from before 1350 rarely survive.

stations.name: The altar
stations.rule: Receive at least once a year, at Easter (canon 21). Canon 1 says the bread is “changed (transsubstantiatio) by divine power into the body”, by a duly ordained priest.
stations.record: A small box like the one pictured held the bread. A yearly floor suggests the council did not expect much more of many people.
stations.limit: A minimum is not a measure, and no register of communions survives to count.
stations.stand: Baptists hold the Lord's Supper to be a symbolic act of remembrance, and that there is “one mediator between God and men”, Christ. That is this site's view. The teaching here is reported as the council's.

claims.claim: “Medieval Christians thought the earth was flat.”
claims.head: The schoolbook said round. The story is modern.
claims.evidence: Aquinas, in the first article of the Summa, uses as his ordinary example that astronomer and physicist can both prove “that the earth, for instance, is round”. He is not arguing it: he assumes his reader agrees. Historian Jeffrey Burton Russell traces the flat-earth story largely to writers of the 1800s.
claims.inference: Among educated people the claim is false. Those who repeat it are repeating a nineteenth-century story about the Middle Ages.
claims.limit: Aquinas speaks for the schools. What a ploughman thought about the shape of the earth is not recorded either way.

options.text: That learned readers could take a round earth for granted.
options.why: He uses it as a plain example in passing. It shows what he expected his readers to accept.

options.text: That every person in Europe knew the earth was round.
options.why: One master's example cannot speak for villagers, and no record of their views was kept.

options.text: That the church had defined the earth's shape as doctrine.
options.why: An example in a discussion of how sciences differ is not a definition by anyone.

claims.claim: “The medieval church forbade ordinary people to read the Bible.”
claims.head: Some bishops did. No ruling for all has been found.
claims.evidence: In 1229 the provincial council of Toulouse said: “We prohibit also that the laity should be permitted to have the books of the Old and New Testaments”, except the Psalter and service books. A synod at Tarragona in 1234 ordered translations burned, and one at Béziers in 1246 denied the laity theological books. These came amid conflict with the Cathars and Waldensians. In 1199 Innocent III banned secret Bible meetings at Metz while saying the desire to study Scripture was not to blame.
claims.inference: The popular claim is too wide, and “it never happened” is false too. Real bans existed, local and aimed at dissent. Far more people were kept from the Bible by the cost of a book and not knowing how to read.
claims.limit: This study read Toulouse through reference works and not the Latin. A statement that no general ban exists rests on what scholars report. It cannot be proved by this study's own search.

test.question: A friend says “the Council of Toulouse proves the church banned the Bible for everyone.” What can the evidence say?

options.text: A real ban, in one province, in a war with dissent. It does not reach everyone.
options.why: Toulouse is a provincial council. A council at Béziers in 1233 reused other parts of its rulings and left this one out, though a synod there in 1246 went its own way against lay books.

options.text: The ban never existed: this is a Protestant invention.
options.why: The canon is real, and the same record shows Tarragona burning translations.

options.text: Yes. A council's word bound the whole Western church.
options.why: A provincial council binds its province. That is the difference this claim blurs.

claims.head: He claimed much. Kings answered.
claims.evidence: The Dictates say he may depose emperors, and Unam Sanctam says every creature must be subject to him. Henry IV took Rome in 1084, and Philip IV's men seized Boniface in 1303. John did hand England to Innocent III in 1213, which is the claim's best case, and it was John's own bargain.
claims.inference: The papacy was a real power, able to shake kings. It did not govern Europe. It could be defied, and the strongest claims came when contested.
claims.limit: This page follows the biggest quarrels. In ordinary years, popes and kings worked together on bishops and taxes, and those years leave less drama and need another study.

test.question: What does the sentence in Unam Sanctam, by itself, establish?

options.why: A document is first of all evidence of what its writer said.

options.text: That Europe's kings obeyed the pope.
options.why: Anagni, one year later, is the answer. A claim is not its own proof.

options.text: That no one took the claim seriously.
options.why: The quarrel ran wider than this one bull, but Philip's side plainly did not wave the claim away.

claims.claim: “It was an age when everyone believed.”
claims.head: Baptism was the norm. Belief is another question.
claims.evidence: Canon 21 sets a penalty for not confessing yearly. Bede's Rædwald kept two altars, and Iceland's law allowed private sacrifice at first. On the other side stand costly lives such as that of Boniface, killed in his old age on mission.
claims.inference: This study takes the medieval rite of baptism to have been the norm among Latin Christians by 1350, with Jews, Muslims in Spain and Sicily, and pagans in Lithuania outside it. That is a fact about an institution. What each person believed cannot be read off it, whether to praise them or to dismiss them.
claims.limit: The record favours rulers, clergy and offenders. An ordinary believing villager, or an ordinary doubting one, rarely leaves a word.

test.question: A canon threatens those who do not confess each year. What follows?

options.text: Some people may not have been doing it, and the rule-makers cared that they should.
options.why: A rule points to a concern. How large the problem was, it does not say.
A failure to confess is not a measure of belief, and the canon gives no number.

options.text: Everyone obeyed, because a council had spoken.
options.why: Rule and practice are the difference this page keeps asking about.

confusedWords.note: A canon shows what its makers wanted. Only other evidence shows what followed.

On this page “baptised” reports the medieval rite. It could be counted, ordered or forced. Faith cannot be, and a record of the first is not a record of the second. The site's own view of baptism is in the panels that say so.
A document claiming authority is evidence for the claim. Power shows when someone tests it.

confusedWords.word: A general and a provincial council
confusedWords.note: A general council spoke for the Western church in that age's reckoning. A provincial one bound its own province.
A rule repeated may mean it was being broken, or only that it was being kept in view. Repetition alone cannot tell which.
Universities mostly grew. A “founding” date is often a later choice among several true events.
In these records “the church” usually means the institution and its officers. The parishioners in the nave left almost no writing.
A schism is a break in communion; a heresy is a teaching judged false. 1054 is usually called a schism, and each side also accused the other of error.
Inquisitors judged; rulers punished. The verdict still decided the punishment.

reach: This is a selection: eleven pairs, eleven places, eleven contests, seven steps between East and West and nine events of crusade and trial, chosen to show the gap between record and practice at its plainest. It is not a census or a narrative history, and the pairs cannot measure how often rules were kept.

The Greek East appears only where it parted from Rome. Spain, Ireland, Italian towns, Hungary, Bohemia and Lithuania are named lightly or not at all. Women appear here far less than they did in that church.

Much of the throne, mission, East and West, and crusade detail comes through reference articles, and each source says so. The canons, statutes, Bede, Aquinas, Gregory, the visitation records and the short crusade selections were read in the English named, and Alcuin's sentence in Latin.
Ranges on the charts run from a source's stated years. Where a range is this study's own, the page says so.

checkNotes.was: [check: Avignonet 1242 and Montségur 1244, with the number burned]
checkNotes.before: In May 1242 men from the Cathar stronghold of Montségur killed the inquisitor William Arnaud and his companions at Avignonet. When Montségur surrendered in March 1244, about two hundred Cathars who would not renounce their faith were burned.
checkNotes.after: In May 1242 men from the Cathar stronghold of Montségur killed the inquisitor William Arnaud and his companions at Avignonet. When Montségur surrendered in March 1244, about two hundred Cathars who would not renounce their faith were burned.
checkNotes.note: Usual accounts from reference works, not read here. The number burned at Montségur is usually given as about 200 (some say 210 or 220).
